question: What were the latest major changes to the laws and regulations governing civil service functioning in and when did they take place?
answer:
The latest major de jure change identified is the Government Service (Amendment) Act, 2026 (Act No. 01 of 2026), which amended the Government Service Act, 2018 by substituting section 37A. The new section 37A creates special provisions on government employees’ conduct and punishment. It treats as misconduct disrupting government work such acts as disobeying lawful orders of superior authorities or government orders/circulars/instructions, obstructing their implementation, collectively abstaining from work without leave or reasonable cause, or preventing another government employee from attending work or performing duties. The listed penalties include demotion to a lower post or lower pay grade, compulsory retirement, and dismissal from service. It also establishes an expedited disciplinary process: a show-cause notice within 7 working days, formation of a three-member inquiry committee within 3 working days where proceedings continue, completion of inquiry within 14 working days with a possible one-time extension of up to 7 working days, recording failures by inquiry committee members in PMIS/dossiers, and appeal or presidential review within 30 working days depending on the authority issuing the punishment.

Before that, a major amendment was the Government Service (Amendment) Act, 2023 (Act No. 18 of 2023). It amended section 1 on the Act’s application, inserted subsection 1(4A), and made selected provisions of the Government Service Act applicable to employees of autonomous bodies, state-owned enterprises, and local government institutions—specifically sections 15 and 41–45. The 2023 amendment also made other textual amendments noted in the Act’s footnotes, including changes to cross-references and insertion of a requirement for consultation with the Commission in one provision.

The underlying framework is the Government Service Act, 2018, which came into force on 1 October 2019 under S.R.O. No. 305-Law/2019 dated 25 September 2019. It consolidated the statutory basis for government service by covering matters such as government control and jurisdiction over employees, merit and open competition in direct recruitment, promotion criteria, pay and benefits, leave, personnel records, welfare, and absorption of surplus employees. It also repealed several earlier laws, including laws on public servants’ retirement, service reorganization and conditions, special provisions for government servants, punctual attendance discipline, dismissal on conviction, and surplus employee absorption.

The snippets explicitly identify the Act’s commencement in 2019, the 2023 amendment, and the 2026 amendment replacing section 37A. question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the quality and efficient processes of the HRMIS ?
answer: The retrieved official sources do not name a dedicated HRMIS reform programme. However, they point to broader ongoing public administration and HR-management reforms that would improve the quality and efficiency of HRMIS-related processes. First, the Government Service Act framework requires the government or competent authority to prepare training policies for improving professional skills and capacity, to prepare career plans for sound manpower management, and to introduce an objective, results-oriented performance audit/evaluation system for public employees. It also authorizes measures for institution-based evaluation to ensure efficiency, accountability, effectiveness and dynamism in government institutions. These provisions imply reforms toward more structured HR data, performance records, career-planning information, and institutional performance information—core inputs for a better HRMIS. Second, the Ministry of Public Administration portal continues to publish and update civil service recruitment notifications and legislative/rules information, including a 2024 amendment to the Bangladesh Civil Service recruitment rules. This reflects continued digitisation and online availability of HR administration information. Third, some government portals show the use of internal e-services and MIS-type platforms, such as TEMIS in the technical education sector, suggesting that MIS-based personnel and institutional information systems are part of the broader public-sector digital administration environment. Overall, based on the retrieved documents, the reform direction is not a single explicitly named HRMIS project, but a combination of legal HR reforms—training policy, career planning, results-based performance evaluation, and institutional evaluation—together with digitised publication and management of HR-related rules, recruitment and service information.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in managing the performance of the civil servants?
answer: Studies of Brazil’s public administration identify several challenges in managing civil servants’ performance: there is no single appraisal model suitable for every public body, so systems must be adapted to legal rules, organizational structures and political conditions. They also need clear performance standards, appropriate objective and subjective indicators, effective evaluator training, multiple sources of assessment, and feedback or performance-monitoring meetings. For the federal civil service specifically, research reports that the appraisal policy remains of limited effectiveness and has low acceptance among public servants; organizational culture, influenced by national culture and formal administrative structures, also strongly affects how performance management works.

Identificou-se que não existe um modelo universal de AD aplicável a toda administração pública e que, em geral, as políticas de AD adotam um modelo baseado nas referências tradicionais da literatura, mesmo que não seja exclusivo ao setor público.

Os resultados apontam que é crucial adaptar abordagens tradicionais diante de aspectos contextuais impostos na implementação, como normas legais, estrutura organizacional e implicações políticas que influenciam a avaliação de desempenho e devem ser considerados no processo de implementação.

Como características das políticas, os resultados enfatizam a necessidade de padrões de desempenho claros e indicadores adequados, tanto objetivos quanto subjetivos, respaldados por treinamento eficaz de avaliadores. Além disso, identificou-se a adoção de múltiplas fontes de avaliação e a importância de reuniões de devolutiva ou de monitoramento do desempenho, mesmo que estas sejam informais.

First, personnel move between the public and private sectors; the government describes recruitment in both directions and notes that individuals may have employment contracts elsewhere. **Inference:** this mobility can make it harder to retain the desired number of civil servants, although the evidence does not quantify turnover or directly identify a retention shortfall. Second, organizational reforms require personnel to be reassigned to match changing needs, with additional training where departments are restructured. The government also directly identifies the quality, efficiency and delivery of public services as continuing challenges. The evidence does not establish specific shortages, pay-related causes or turnover rates.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the retention of civil service personnel?
answer: Cambodia’s public-administration reform agenda includes measures that could help retain civil servants, although the cited evidence does not explicitly identify them as a retention strategy. The reforms include raising civil-service pay toward a livable wage, particularly benefiting lower-paid staff; simplifying salary scales and paying salaries electronically and on time; and improving human-resource management through computerisation, pilot performance-management systems and civil-servant training requirements. The agenda also includes institutional rationalisation and restructuring. **Inference:** Better pay, more reliable payment and stronger career-management practices could make civil-service employment more attractive. The cited reform programme covers 2015–2018, so this evidence alone does not establish which measures remain ongoing today.

answer: Cambodia is pursuing HRMIS modernization through a roadmap for a phased transition to a full-suite HRMIS. question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in implementing the desired compensation policy?
answer: Colombia’s public service faces six main challenges in implementing its desired compensation policy: (1) a dispersed salary structure with only small pay differences between adjacent grades; (2) too many grades—110 in the national executive branch—which hinder mobility; (3) different salary systems across entities, creating disparities and inequity; (4) limited scope for variable or results-based pay, with existing mechanisms failing to reward effort, individual or group performance, learning, and skills development; (5) comparatively low pay for senior public servants relative to other sectors, making recruitment and retention harder; and (6) the absence of a competency framework and weak links between performance appraisal, training, career development, and compensation.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: Colombia’s documented efforts include a reform of career civil servants’ performance appraisal and training for those who conduct it. CNSC Agreement 565 of 2016 replaced Agreement 137 of 2010 and placed greater emphasis on behavioural performance and the management of organisational units, with the aim of linking individual performance to institutional results and citizen satisfaction. More recently, the CNSC offered a four-week virtual course beginning 31 October 2024, “Un cambio de paradigma: de la Evaluación de Desempeño a la Gestión del Desempeño,” for officials serving as evaluators in the performance-evaluation process established under Agreement 617 of 2018. The CNSC describes that process as an objective, ongoing assessment of individual contributions and conduct against institutional goals. **Inferred:** the course supports a shift toward continuous performance management; its existence does not establish a government-wide reform programme. A government review also calls for complementary measures to measure productivity and improve performance, but the cited evidence does not establish that those measures have been implemented.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the retention of civil service personnel?

Earlier reforms also included salary-related measures such as revalorisations, index bonuses, promotions, and unblocking advancement indices for civil servants. Together, these reforms aim to make the public service better managed, more predictable, fairer, better trained, and more attractive for personnel to remain in service.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in retaining the desired numbers and quality of the civil service personnel?
answer: Estonia’s main retention challenges are keeping public-service pay competitive, managing uncertainty from organisational restructuring, and sustaining the required skills and service quality with a smaller civil service as the population ages and shrinks. In 2024, public-service pay grew by 4%, compared with 8.1% across the Estonian labour market; managers’ pay in particular lagged behind private-sector pay for work of comparable complexity. Several ministries identified restructuring and the uncertainty it created as reasons for voluntary departures. Public-service roles also have relatively high educational requirements, making competition for skills valued by private employers relevant to retaining personnel. Inference: population decline may further constrain recruitment, but the cited evidence states the need to deliver high-quality, accessible services with a smaller civil service, not a measured recruitment shortfall.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the retention of civil service personnel?
answer: Estonia’s reform plans address retention in two ways. The government was preparing proposals to make it easier to hire and retain highly qualified senior civil servants. A recently established top-management support unit was to help ministries and agencies recruit senior staff and support senior appointees through career planning and contract management; the proposals were described as forthcoming, not implemented. Separately, the government’s personnel-policy plans called for analysing and developing career mobility across government bodies and with international organisations, considering rotation and succession planning, and improving career paths between specialised services and other agencies. Possible implementation tools included a mobility-support plan and amendments to the Public Service Act. The retention benefit of these broader career-mobility measures is inferred: the cited policy describes career-development measures but does not establish that they have improved retention.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in the recruitment process?

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the civil service recruitment process?
answer: Ongoing reforms aimed at improving Ghana's civil service recruitment process include: (1) Full operationalisation and rollout of the Human Resource Management Information System (HRMIS) across all Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs) and Metropolitan, Municipal, and District Assemblies (MMDAs), with 130 Public Service Organisations onboarded and 95% of staff on the mechanised payroll integrated; (2) Completion of HRMIS rollout and a comprehensive Human Resource Audit planned for 2026; (3) Development of an updated job catalog and robust competency framework for key public sector job families to define core and technical competencies; (4) Operationalising a meritocratic recruitment process through publication of job descriptions, salary ranges, and selection criteria; (5) Guaranteeing more transparent recruitment practices to improve public service delivery and reinforce public trust; (6) Establishment of an independent oversight body to ensure compliance with transparency and merit-based standards; and (7) Strengthening establishment controls and moving toward strategic workforce planning to identify gaps between current and future workforce needs. These reforms are grounded in both the 2026 Budget Statement and World Bank recommendations, collectively addressing transparency, merit-based selection, digital HR infrastructure, workforce planning, and independent oversight.

Based on the available evidence, the following ongoing and planned reforms aimed at improving Ghana's civil service recruitment process have been identified:

1. **Operationalisation of a meritocratic recruitment process**: The World Bank assessment on Ghana's public sector wage bill recommends — and describes as a reform priority — operationalising a meritocratic recruitment process through the publication of job descriptions, salary ranges, and selection criteria (Measure 2.3: 'Guarantee more transparent recruitment practices to improve public service delivery while reinforcing public trust and engagement').

2. **Development of a job catalogue and competency framework**: Measure 2.2 calls for developing an updated job catalog and a robust competency framework for key public sector job families, so that each position's core and technical competencies are clearly defined — a foundational component for meritocratic, transparent recruitment.

3. **Strengthening establishment controls**: Measure 2.1 involves moving toward strategic workforce planning to identify gaps between the current workforce and future human capital needs, based on robust HR data, which underpins any reformed recruitment process.

4. **Establishment of an independent oversight body for recruitment**: Measure 2.4 recommends establishing an independent body to oversee recruitment processes, ensuring compliance with transparency and merit-based standards, and to further depoliticise the civil service.

5. **HRMIS rollout and digital HR reform**: The 2026 Budget Statement reports that the Human Resource Management Information System (HRMIS) has been fully operationalised across four key Central Management Agencies, with 130 Public Service Organisations onboarded and approximately 95% of staff on the Government of Ghana mechanised payroll integrated into the system. In 2026, the Public Services Commission plans to complete the HRMIS rollout to all MDAs and MMDAs and conduct a comprehensive Human Resource Audit — described as part of the 'HR reform agenda', which supports digitalisation of HR processes including recruitment.

These reforms collectively address transparency, merit-based selection, digital infrastructure for HR management, workforce planning, and independent oversight of recruitment in Ghana's civil service.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in implementing the desired compensation policy?
answer: Ghana's public service faces several key challenges in implementing its desired compensation policy, notably the Single Spine Pay Policy (SSPP): (1) Unsustainable and volatile wage bill growth, undermining fiscal performance and sustainability; (2) No effective linkage between compensation and employee performance or productivity, reducing incentives; (3) Outdated job evaluation (last conducted in 2008), leading to frequent demands for grade reviews and affecting industrial relations; (4) Over-reliance on allowances rather than base pay, fostering opacity, inequity, and regional disparities, and creating pension-related trade-offs; (5) Compensation decisions are often reactive and politically driven, rather than based on strategic workforce planning; (6) Wage bill growth outpaces employment growth, indicating inefficiency; (7) Lack of a long-term policy framework, inconsistent recordkeeping, and antiquated information systems, making wage forecasting difficult and contributing to payroll irregularities; (8) Difficulty attracting and retaining critical and scarce skills, prompting the need for Market Premiums; (9) Regional disparities in remuneration and lack of transparency in compensation reporting. All points are directly grounded in official government budget documents and independent assessments.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the civil service compensation policy?

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: Ongoing reforms to improve performance management of Ghanaian civil servants include: (1) Experimentation with new approaches to the appraisal system, as planned by the Office of the Head of Civil Service (OHCS) in the coming year; (2) Continued rollout and expansion of Performance Agreements for Chief Directors, Heads of Departments, Directors/Analogous grades, and Heads of Missions, including annual signing, evaluation, and training on completion of templates; (3) Phased implementation of the Public Services Commission's (PSC) Performance Management Policy and new appraisal instruments, with annual appraisals, mid-year reviews, and performance rewards/sanctions for all public servants since 2012; (4) Training and capacity building for HR managers and supervisors in administering the new appraisal instruments; (5) Efforts to align individual and team performance objectives with institutional and national development goals; (6) Improvement of staff data management to establish an accurate Civil Service database for better policy implementation. These reforms are documented in the OHCS 2022–2025 Strategic Plan, the PSC Performance Management Policy, and recent monitoring reports.
quote:
The following ongoing reforms aimed at improving performance management of civil servants in Ghana have been identified from the evidence:

1. **Experimentation with new appraisal approaches (OHCS, 2025):** The Office of the Head of Civil Service (OHCS) has included in its workplan for the near term the experimentation with new approaches to the appraisal system, as referenced in an IGC monitoring study (2025). This signals active reform at the system design level.

2. **Continued rollout of Performance Agreements for Category 'A' Post Holders:** Under the OHCS Strategic Medium-Term Development Plan (SMTDP) 2022–2025, Chief Directors, Heads of Departments, and Directors/analogous grades are required to sign Performance Agreements at the start of the year and participate in end-of-year evaluations. The number of officers covered has been growing incrementally (e.g., from 35 to 38 Chief Directors evaluated between 2019 and 2020).

3. **Extension of Performance Management to Foreign Missions:** Since 2019, the OHCS extended Performance Management arrangements to Ghana's Foreign Missions, with Heads of Missions and A1 Officers trained and signing agreements with the Chief Director, endorsed by the Minister of MoFARI.

4. **Phased implementation of the Public Services Commission's new Performance Management System (PMS):** The PSC's Performance Management Policy (approved by Cabinet) established a phased rollout: Phase 1 (2010) involved design and validation of a new Staff Performance Appraisal Format and Practitioner's Manual; Phase 2 (2011) piloted the system with Directors and Deputy Directors; Phase 3 (from 2012 onwards) extended annual appraisal using new instruments to all public servants and introduced Institutional Performance Assessments. The PSC's performance appraisal form (ME-SPRAS01) operationalises this system as a six-phase annual cycle.

5. **Staff data management improvement:** The OHCS SMTDP 2022–2025 identifies the lack of accurate staff data as a major challenge and flags work to establish an accurate Civil Service database, which underpins effective performance management implementation.

In summary, the principal ongoing reform is the OHCS-led effort to redesign and refine the appraisal system (including new approaches being piloted), alongside the continued deepening of Performance Agreements coverage and the broader PSC-led performance management framework for all civil servants.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in ensuring the desired level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: The key challenges faced by the Ghana Civil Service in ensuring the desired level and quality of training are: (1) uncoordinated training programmes and courses that are sometimes not directly and immediately relevant to the career paths and job schedules of staff, leading to misalignment between training and actual needs; (2) unsustainability of training programmes due to limited training votes (funding constraints), which undermines the scale and frequency of training; (3) financial resource constraints that limit officers' access to skills training, particularly in diagnostic and analytical skills; (4) gaps in basic and analytical skills, with some officers struggling to implement existing systems and limited use of analytical tools for performance assessment; (5) resistance to change and incomplete integration of reforms, as some sector ministries have not fully realised the benefits of capacity development due to resistance; and (6) an aging workforce and succession planning gaps, which place additional demands on training and development systems. These challenges are documented in official Civil Service policy documents and recent performance and research reports.
quote:

1. **Uncoordinated training programmes**: Training courses are sometimes not directly and immediately relevant to the career paths and job schedules of staff, leading to misalignment between training offered and actual needs.

2. **Unsustainability due to limited training votes (funding)**: Training programmes are undermined by insufficient budgetary allocations ('limited training votes'), making it difficult to sustain programmes at the required scale and frequency. This is confirmed by both the 2017 and 2021 OHCS Training Policy documents as the two primary identified challenges.

3. **Financial resource constraints limiting access to skills training**: As noted in the 2025 IGC research report, financial resources hinder officers from undertaking training that equips them with diagnostic and analytical skills yielding higher performance.

6. **Aging workforce and succession planning gaps**: The aging workforce at senior levels creates urgency for structured succession planning and knowledge transfer, placing additional demands on training and development systems.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in retaining the desired numbers and quality of the civil service personnel?
answer: The key challenges faced by the Ghana Civil Service in retaining the desired numbers and quality of personnel are: (1) uncompetitive conditions of service, with many officers resigning for better pay and benefits elsewhere; (2) an aging workforce, especially at senior levels, with nearly 30% of Chief Executive Officers and Assistant Chief Executive Officers approaching retirement age, creating risks of institutional knowledge loss; (3) increased resignations among the professional cadre, including officers leaving to pursue higher academic qualifications; (4) urgent need for structured succession planning and knowledge transfer, as the workforce is concentrated in the 40–59 age range; (5) difficulty attracting and retaining younger professionals to ensure future leadership; (6) lack of a long-term public employment policy framework and weak HR data management systems, which undermine strategic workforce planning and retention; and (7) general constraints typical of a developing middle-income country, such as fiscal and labour-market limitations. These challenges are documented in the 2024 Civil Service Annual Performance Report and corroborated by World Bank assessments.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: Laos’s 2015 Civil Servant Law sets out a framework for improving civil-service training. It calls for continuous, profession-specific training matched to agencies’ practical needs and informed by performance assessments. Training is to align with socioeconomic, human-resource and civil-service development strategies; incorporate new technology and improved foreign-language skills; and meet quality standards appropriate to its target groups. Civil-service management bodies are responsible for setting training and development strategies, plans, programmes and projects. These are requirements in the legal framework; the cited evidence does not establish which measures are currently being implemented as ongoing reforms.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in retaining the desired numbers and quality of the civil service personnel?
answer: Historical evidence from Laos identifies several challenges to maintaining the desired number and quality of civil servants: low wages and limited interest in civil-service jobs among younger people; difficulty retaining trained teachers, with few teacher-training graduates remaining in the profession; and gaps in administrative qualifications, with many administrators relying on learning-by-doing rather than professional credentials. The evidence also identifies weaknesses in workforce planning and management, a need for sustainable training, and unresolved personnel lists and procedures for removing former employees, which make staffing numbers harder to establish reliably. question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in improving and maintaining the coverage of the HRM systems?
answer: The main challenge is the limited coverage of the Personnel Information Management System (PIMS). Although it is deployed in central ministries and agencies and provincial governments, it covers only about 50% of civil servants; district-level civil servants and teachers are the principal gaps. Coverage falls below 25% of the wider public-sector workforce because police, armed forces, and contractual and casual workers are outside the system. Limitations in PIMS’s functions and data architecture also prevent it from operating as a full HRMIS, hampering the government’s ability to manage civil servants and analyse and forecast the wage bill.

question: What were the latest major changes to the laws and regulations governing civil service functioning in and when did they take place?
answer: Morocco’s civil service is still principally governed by the General Statute of the Civil Service adopted by Dahir No. 1.58.008 of 24 February 1958. The retrieved evidence indicates that this framework has not been subject to a comprehensive, deep reform since 1958. The more recent changes have instead been partial legal and regulatory adjustments. After the 2011 Constitution, the civil service framework was aligned with principles such as merit, transparency and equal opportunity, including broader reliance on competitive examinations as the main recruitment route, new promotion conditions emphasizing performance, restrictions on holding multiple public functions/remunerations, redeployment as a human-resource management tool, and authorization of fixed-term contractual recruitment for defined missions. The clearest recent dated regulatory package concerns contractual recruitment: Decree No. 2.15.770 of 9 August 2016 set the conditions and modalities for recruitment by contract in public administrations; in 2017, implementing instruments addressed recruitment competitions, standard contract models, and remuneration/allowances for contracted experts and agents. In addition, ministry performance documentation indicates that broader administration-reform measures, including reforms related to senior appointments and positions of responsibility, were being implemented from 2021. Overall, the latest major changes appear to have taken place mainly in the post-2011 period, especially 2016–2017 for contractual recruitment and recruitment procedures, with further administrative reform implementation from 2021, but without a full replacement of the 1958 General Statute.

question: What were the latest major changes to the laws and regulations governing civil service functioning in and when did they take place?
answer: The latest major changes identified were approved in 2025 and focused on modernizing Mozambique's Public Administration and strengthening civil-service human-resource management. A later legislative listing for November 2025 confirms that Decree No. 39/2025 approved the Regulation of the Staff Planning Subsystem, and also records Decree No. 38/2025 revoking article 10 of the Statute of the Public Manager. Thus, the main recent changes took place in 2025, with Council of Ministers approval reported in September 2025 and formal legal publication of related decrees in November 2025.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the civil service compensation policy?

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: Nigeria’s federal civil-service reform replaces the Annual Performance Evaluation Report (APER) with a Performance Management System (PMS) for Federal Ministries, Extra-Ministerial Departments and Agencies. The PMS is intended to set employee goals and objectives, track, assess and report individual performance, and emphasize measurable performance objectives, targets and relevant competencies. It also provides for results-oriented performance management and training, with annual individual goals following the finalisation of MDA institutional and departmental goals and targets.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer:
Nigeria’s civil-service training reforms centre on the capacity-building and talent-management pillar of the Federal Civil Service Strategy and Implementation Plan 2021–2025 (FCSSIP-25). A report states that three programmes have been redesigned and relaunched to improve their effectiveness: the Leadership Enhancement and Development Programme (LEAD-P), the Structured Mandatory and Assessment-based Training Programme (SMAT-P), and the Induction Programme. The agenda also includes institutionalising capability building and talent management, an annual capacity-building programme for Permanent Secretaries, and planned e-learning delivery of induction training.

Separately, the National e-Government Masterplan proposes training tailored to civil servants’ roles, including basic ICT/e-Government education, priority training for senior leaders and higher officials, and specialist programmes for ICT/e-Government experts. It also proposes Nigeria-specific courses, better programmes and facilities at existing training institutions, dedicated e-Government training institutions under the FMoC, and assessment and certification to recognise skills. These masterplan measures are proposals; the cited evidence does not establish that they have all been implemented.

The 2025 Omnibus Rules on Appointments and Other Human Resource Actions streamline and digitize HR processes, including digital signatures, recognition of electronic eligibility documents, simplified requirements, and earlier vacancy publication. The updated Rules on Administrative Cases in the Civil Service integrate recent laws, jurisprudence, and technology-enabled procedures to support fairer and more timely accountability processes. The revised SALN rules introduce simplified digital processes to strengthen transparency and compliance. Together, these reforms reinforce meritocracy, accountability, integrity, and modernization, all of which are core enablers of effective performance management.

The current reforms appear to build on this trajectory by shifting emphasis toward digitalized HR administration, stronger accountability systems, quality and efficiency in public service delivery, and a more competent and motivated workforce.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the civil service recruitment process?
answer: Senegal is implementing a comprehensive set of ongoing reforms to improve the civil service recruitment process. The centerpiece is the drafting of a new General Civil Service Statute, with a four-day workshop in August 2024 examining the initial draft. This reform aims to unify and modernize recruitment rules for both state and territorial civil services, shifting towards results-based management. National consultations involving civil society, professional organizations, and public administration stakeholders are informing the reform process. The Ministry has also digitalized recruitment through an online application platform (https://emploi-fpublique.sec.gouv.sn), matching candidates to ministry needs based on various criteria. Institutional strengthening includes the creation of the Direction de la Gestion prévisionnelle des Effectifs, des Emplois et des Compétences (DGEEC) with a dedicated Division du Recrutement, responsible for identifying HR needs and managing recruitment. Additionally, the dematerialization of HR procedures, such as grade advancement commissions, is being extended to all civil servants, supporting the broader modernization and professionalization of public HR management.
quote:
Based on the available evidence from Senegal's Ministry of Public Service (Ministère de la Fonction Publique et de la Réforme du Service public), the following ongoing reforms aimed at improving civil service recruitment have been identified:

1. **New General Civil Service Statute (Nouveau Statut Général de la Fonction Publique)**: In August 2024, Minister Olivier Boucal launched a formal drafting process for a new general civil service law. A workshop (27–30 August 2024) examined the 'draft 0' of the project. This reform aims to unify and modernise the rules governing both state and territorial civil service, including recruitment frameworks. It marks a shift toward results-based management ('gestion axée sur les résultats'). The final text will also address territorial civil service recruitment rules in collaboration with the Ministry for Territorial Collectivities.

2. **National Consultations on Public Service Reform (Concertations nationales pour la réforme du Service public)**: Officially launched (referenced on the Ministry's homepage as of 2025), these national consultations gather input from civil society, professional organisations, and public administration stakeholders to inform the reform of recruitment and other civil service functions.

3. **Digitalisation of Recruitment (Dématérialisation du recrutement)**: An online job application platform (https://emploi-fpublique.sec.gouv.sn) has been established for managing civil service recruitment demand. Applications are submitted digitally and matched against ministry needs, with criteria including profile, age, gender, and disability status.

4. **Strengthened Institutional Framework for Recruitment**: The March 2023 decree reorganising the Ministry created a dedicated 'Direction de la Gestion prévisionnelle des Effectifs, des Emplois et des Compétences' (DGEEC) with a 'Division du Recrutement', mandated to identify HR needs, conduct recruitment processes, and develop workforce projections. The same decree mandates contribution to the digitalisation of public services.

5. **Dématérialisation of Administrative Commissions**: Since 2021, grade advancement commissions for teaching staff have been dematerialised, extended to the health sector in 2023, with a plan to generalise to all civil servants from 2024. While focused on career management, this digital transformation is part of the broader recruitment and HR modernisation agenda.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in implementing the desired compensation policy?
answer: Key challenges in implementing Senegal's desired civil service compensation policy, as evidenced primarily by a World Bank assessment, include: (1) Erosion of real public sector pay relative to the private sector, as civil service salary adjustments have tracked minimum wage trends rather than market rates, reducing competitiveness; (2) Rigidity of the 'grille indiciaire' pay structure, limiting flexibility to tailor compensation to job requirements or reward performance; (3) Proliferation and inequity of allowances (indemnités), which constitute a large share of total compensation and create psychological and lobbying issues, as nearly all groups seek special treatment; (4) Competitive disadvantage versus parastatals, with high-skilled civil servants incentivized to leave for better-paying positions in public enterprises or the private sector; (5) HR management dysfunctions, as evidenced by a 2012 audit revealing widespread issues in state HR management, which implicitly affect compensation administration. Note: Most evidence is from the mid-1980s World Bank assessment, with more recent systematic compensation-specific evaluations not found in the retrieved evidence.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the civil service compensation policy?
answer: Senegal is pursuing several ongoing reforms to improve its civil service compensation policy. These reforms are aligned with the Programme Sénégal Emergent and the broader modernization of public administration. Specific pay reform provisions are not yet detailed in the available evidence, but compensation policy is a central part of the statutory overhaul.

A steering committee (comité de pilotage) was established by primatorial decree n°16878 of 7 October 2013. The study identified major dysfunctions: proliferation of opaque allowances and bonuses (primes and indemnités) outside any regulatory framework and not appearing on pay slips, representing 15–100% of base salary; a fragmented and incoherent regulatory framework; and structural weaknesses in the grille indiciaire. The strategic recommendations included: (a) renovation of the remuneration system (rénovation du système de rémunération); (b) modernisation and reliability of workforce and payroll management (modernisation et fiabilisation de la gestion des effectifs et de la solde); (c) strengthening the legal and statutory framework (renforcement du dispositif juridique et statutaire); (d) rationalisation of HR management; and (e) improved institutional monitoring of workforce and wage bill management (amélioration du dispositif institutionnel de suivi en matière de gestion des effectifs et de la masse salariale).

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: Senegal is undertaking a comprehensive set of reforms to improve the level and quality of training in the civil service, anchored by the Stratégie nationale de formation continue des agents de l'État (SNFC 2025-2029). This strategy, validated in December 2024, covers all 187 corps of the civil service (including special and territorial statutes) and aims to professionalise human resources, renew financing for continuous training, align partner training offers with national priorities, and ensure that no civil servant goes a year without training. The SNFC is operationalised through defined budgets, indicators, timelines, and risk mitigation measures, overseen by a dedicated follow-up committee. Complementary reforms include: modernisation of the ENA (École Nationale d'Administration) with a new master's degree, online registration, and updated entrance exams; the creation of the Académie de Leadership Ndatté Yalla to address gender gaps in management training; restructuring of the CNFA (Centre National de Formation et d'Action) to address institutional weaknesses; establishment of the CNFPLF (Centre national de la Fonction publique locale et de la Formation) for local civil service training, including e-learning facilities and legal framework updates; and a foundational skills audit (2015-2016) that informed the SNFC. These reforms collectively aim to modernise, professionalise, and make training more accessible and relevant across Senegal's civil service.

Based on the available evidence from Senegal's Ministry of Public Service website (fonctionpublique.gouv.sn), the following ongoing reforms aimed at improving and maintaining coverage of the HRM system have been identified:

The objective is to give the State better control over headcount and payroll, make personnel data reliable, available and accessible in real time, and ensure coherent follow-up of personnel data between the MEF central systems and sectoral systems.

2. **E-carrière digital service**: An active e-government service allowing civil servants to track their career administrative acts online, representing a digitalisation of individual HRM processes.

3. **New General Civil Service Statute reform**: Under decree n°2024-962 of 8 April 2024, a 'draft 0' of a new general civil service law (statut général de la Fonction publique) has been prepared, aiming to unify rules for the State civil service and territorial civil service, modernise the administration, and shift to results-based management.

4. **Informatised Gender-Sensitive Monitoring and Evaluation System (SSE)**: Supported by the PRIEEG project (Projet de Renforcement institutionnel pour l'Équité et l'Égalité de Genre au Sénégal), an IT-based performance monitoring platform has been put in place for the Ministry of Public Service to support results-based management (GAR) of HRM programmes.

5. **Stratégie nationale de formation continue (SNFC) 2025–2029**: A National Continuous Training Strategy covering 187 corps of the civil service (including special statutes and territorial civil service) was validated and its action plan finalised (February 2026 workshop in Saly/Mbour), aiming to professionalise HR management across government.

6. **Réseau des gestionnaires RH de l'Administration publique (HR managers network)**: An initiative to create a network of HR managers across public administration, sharing best practices; a capacity-building workshop was held in December 2022.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in improving and maintaining the transparency of the HRMIS systems?
answer: Senegal's public service faces several key challenges in improving and maintaining the transparency of its HRMIS systems, as evidenced by the rationale for the unified personnel file project and audit findings. These include: (1) fragmentation of personnel data across multiple systems and structures (payroll, pensions, sectoral HR, and central finance), impeding consolidated oversight and real-time access; (2) lack of reliable, real-time data, with previous systems failing to ensure data integrity and accessibility; (3) dysfunctions revealed by audits, such as ghost workers and irregular registrations, undermining data credibility; (4) weak coordination and tracking between central and sectoral systems, leading to poor synchronisation; (5) institutional capacity gaps, such as the absence of dedicated HR/legal cadres, which contributed to governance weaknesses; and (6) limited control over headcount and payroll, making it difficult to verify and manage the civil service workforce. All these challenges are directly cited in the evidence as drivers for the ongoing unified personnel file initiative.
quote:
Based on the available evidence, the key challenges Senegal's public service has faced in improving and maintaining the transparency of its HRMIS systems include:

1. **Data fragmentation across multiple structures and systems**: The unified personnel file (fichier unifié) project was created precisely because data on state personnel were 'disséminées entre plusieurs structures' (scattered across multiple structures), including separate systems for payroll (GIRAFE), pension management, sectoral HR systems (MIRADOR), and the MEF's central systems. Achieving coherent, real-time data required interconnecting these siloed systems.

2. **Lack of reliable, real-time data**: The stated objectives of the fichier unifié explicitly highlight the need to 'rendre fiables, disponibles et accessibles en temps réel les données du personnel de l'État' — implying that, prior to this initiative, data were neither reliable nor accessible in real time.

3. **Dysfunctions identified through audits (ghost workers and HR irregularities)**: The 2012 physical and biometric audit ('audit physique et biométrique des agents de l'État') revealed 'beaucoup de dysfonctionnements dans la gestion des ressources humaines de l'État', pointing to irregularities such as ghost workers and mismanagement in the personnel files.

4. **Weak coherent tracking between central and sectoral systems**: There was a persistent challenge in ensuring 'un suivi plus cohérent des données du personnel entre les systèmes centraux du MEF et les systèmes sectoriels', indicating poor synchronisation between the Ministry of Finance's central systems and ministry/agency-level HR databases.

5. **Absence of dedicated HR/legal cadres**: The 2023 decree creating a cadre of legal affairs civil servants noted that the absence of such a dedicated cadre contributed to the dysfunctions observed in HR management, suggesting that institutional capacity gaps also undermined HRMIS governance and transparency.

6. **Limited control over headcount and payroll mass**: One of the core drivers for the unified file was to give the state 'une plus grande maîtrise sur ses effectifs et sa masse salariale', implying prior difficulties in controlling and verifying the size and cost of the civil service — a fundamental transparency challenge.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the quality and efficient processes of the HRMIS ?
answer: Senegal's principal ongoing reform to improve HRMIS quality and efficiency is the Fichier Unifié des Données du Personnel de l'État (Unified State Personnel Data File) project. This reform consolidates all State personnel data into a single, shared database, integrating systems such as payroll, public finance management, pensions, personnel administration, HR management, the national ID card system, and sectoral HR systems. The unified file is based on a single-writer/multiple-readers principle for each data type, which enhances data quality, reliability, and real-time accessibility, and reduces duplication and inconsistency. The reform aims to give the State greater control over workforce numbers and the wage bill, ensure coherent data tracking between central and sectoral systems, and support more advanced management solutions. These efforts directly address previous recommendations to rationalize fragmented databases and introduce biometric identification, as highlighted in earlier PEFA assessments.
quote:
The principal ongoing reform aimed at improving the quality and efficiency of the HRMIS in Senegal is the **Fichier Unifié des Données du Personnel de l'État** (Unified State Personnel Data File) project, described on the Ministry of Civil Service website (FY2025). This reform has the following key features:

1. **Consolidated personnel database**: A single, shared data management system integrating personnel data currently dispersed across multiple structures.
2. **Integration with the payroll system** (*système de gestion de la solde des agents de la fonction publique*), the public finance management system, the pension management system, sectoral HR systems, and the national ID card system.
3. **Data quality improvement**: The objective is to make personnel data reliable, available, and accessible in real time ('rendre fiables, disponibles et accessibles en temps réel les données du personnel').
4. **Single-writer/multiple-readers principle**: Each type of data has one authoritative source ('écrivain unique et lecteurs multiples'), reducing duplication and inconsistency.
5. **Better control of headcount and wage bill**: Enabling the State to have greater mastery over its workforce numbers and wage bill ('plus grande maîtrise sur ses effectifs et sa masse salariale').
6. **Coherent data tracking** between the MEF's central systems and sectoral systems.

An earlier (2009) PEFA assessment had also recommended rationalization of the two then-separate personnel databases (Civil Service Agency and Bureau of General Accounting) and the introduction of a biometric identification system and HRMIS as priority milestones — reforms that the current fichier unifié project appears to be addressing.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the civil service compensation policy?
answer: Sweden’s documented efforts to improve central-government compensation policy combine collective-agreement updates with support for local wage-setting. In the 2025 bargaining round, the Swedish Agency for Government Employers concluded new salary agreements with OFR/S,P,O and Seko, and employment-conditions agreements with those organisations and Saco-S. The negotiations also produced changes to central collective agreements, including a salary top-up for reserve officers. To improve local pay decisions, the agency provides guidance, seminars and training; produces shared state-sector salary statistics for analysis and negotiations; and offers Analyskraft, a tool that lets employers analyse their own pay and compare it with relevant reference statistics. These measures are intended to make local wage formation more effective and link pay-setting to organisational results.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in managing the performance of the civil servants?
answer: The available evidence concerns Swedish agency heads, not the civil service as a whole. These are respondents’ views in a 2003 report, not a current assessment of challenges across Sweden’s civil service.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in implementing the desired compensation policy?
answer: Uzbekistan’s public-service compensation policy faces several challenges identified by the World Bank: compensation levels appeared low relative to comparator countries; the growing public-sector wage bill created fiscal-affordability concerns; pressure to raise salaries for particular worker categories and the creation of new ministries and agencies without a clear roadmap increased wage-bill pressure; and multiple allowances were not adequately linked to staff performance and productivity. question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the civil service compensation policy?
answer: Uzbekistan’s ongoing reform aims to establish a unified civil-service remuneration system that links pay to performance, qualifications and position category. Under the Civil Service Development Strategy to 2030, the government tasked the Ministry of Economy and Finance, the Ministry of Employment and Poverty Reduction, and the Civil Service Development Agency with submitting a draft presidential decree by 1 November 2025. The proposed change would determine official salaries from 1 January 2026 under a common principle that considers work experience, academic and qualification levels, performance and other indicators. Earlier reform measures also sought to eliminate pay differences between ministries and agencies and link material incentives to key performance indicators, professional competencies, and the complexity and responsibility of duties. Separately, the World Bank has recommended a common grading and salary framework and incorporating bonuses and allowances into base pay; these are recommendations, not established elements of the planned decree.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: Uzbekistan’s ongoing reform aims to make civil servants’ performance assessments more consistent and competency-based.
